title: Kunti at the river
hook: a frightened young mother sets her shining newborn on the river, and plants a seed the whole epic will follow
carry: karma: every act is a seed

segments.voice: Yesterday, young Pritha spoke Durvasa's mantra to the rising sun, and Surya answered. The sun, greeted as a god each morning.

A baby is born in secret, already dressed for battle. The Mahabharata says he's born wearing armor that's part of his own body, with bright earrings in his ears, shining like his father, the sun. Any newborn would be scandal enough for an unmarried girl in a king's house. This one glows. There's no hiding him in a corner. And his mother is still very young, still a daughter under her father's roof.
screen: `BORN IN SECRET.` → `ARMOR AND EARRINGS.` → `SHINING LIKE THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Kunti's choice is quick in the telling, and heavy in the hearing. Afraid of what her family and the world will say, she places her newborn son in a basket and sets it on the river. A later book tells the scene again at length: she weeps over the basket, asks the gods of the waters, the sky and the earth to keep him safe, and says whoever finds him will be blessed to raise him. Then the current carries him away, wrapped in his father's armor. Notice the word the text chooses. It doesn't call her cruel. It calls her afraid, and lets us watch her grief. Now here's the teaching Hindus hear in this story. Karma. The word simply means action, and Hindu teaching says every action is a seed: it bears fruit, sometimes at once, sometimes years later. Karma isn't a god keeping score, or a punishment dropped from the sky. It's how actions ripen. Many teachers read the whole Mahabharata as a story of karma ripening, and Kunti's basket is one of its biggest seeds. A secret kept out of fear will grow into a man who doesn't know his mother, facing his own brothers across a field. The poem follows that seed a very long way, and it never stops grieving with Kunti while it does. Karma isn't a verdict on who she is. It's the plain truth that what she did on the riverbank will meet her again. That's why Hindu teachers ask us to take small choices seriously: not out of fear, but because a seed is still small enough to choose.
screen: `SHE SETS HIM ON THE RIVER.` · `THE TEXT SAYS: AFRAID.` · `KARMA: ACTION.` · `NOT A PUNISHMENT. A SEED.` · then, large: `KARMA: EVERY ACT IS A SEED.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus end their worship, and some end the day, by offering everything they did to God, with a verse from the Bhagavata Purana: whatever I've done, with body, speech, mind or senses, I offer it all to Narayana. Try it tonight, slowly, one act at a time. If you don't pray, simply name three things you did today, and ask of each one: what might this grow into?
Karna's abandonment. A son born shining in armor and earrings, set adrift by a frightened mother who blessed him as he went.
Your line: karma, every act is a seed. Kunti's has just gone down the river. Tomorrow: who is waiting downstream?
